title: 03 — Data Processing Types
html:
03 — Data Processing Types

The one idea: every kind of data processing is an answer to three questions — how fresh must the result be, how much of the data do I touch each run, and what happens if a run fails halfway. Name the answers precisely (micro-batch, incremental, CDC, merge, at-least-once) and most design arguments resolve themselves.

1. The map

Processing types are not one list; they are several independent axes. A single pipeline picks one value on each axis.

Axis Options Chapter section
Latency / execution model Batch, micro-batch, continuous streaming §2
Workload shape OLTP, OLAP §3
Where transformation happens ETL, ELT, reverse ETL §4
How much source data per run Full load, incremental load, CDC §5
How the target is written Append, overwrite, merge/upsert §6
Overall architecture Lambda, Kappa, unified (lakehouse) §7
How it is invoked Scheduled, event-triggered, interactive/ad hoc §8
Stream memory Stateless, stateful §9
Time grouping Tumbling, sliding, session windows §10
Failure semantics At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once §11
Re-running history Backfill, reprocessing §12

Example description of one pipeline using these axes: "An hourly micro-batch ELT job that ingests CDC from SQL Server with at-least-once delivery and merges into a silver Delta table; idempotent, so reprocessing is safe." Every word in that sentence carries a design decision.

2. Batch, micro-batch and streaming

---
title: Execution models — batch, micro-batch, event-at-a-time
---
flowchart TB
    subgraph B["Batch"]
        B1["Data accumulates all day"] --> B2["One big run at 02:00"] --> B3["Result ready by 03:00"]
    end
    subgraph MB["Micro-batch"]
        M1["Events arrive continuously"] --> M2["Small batch every N seconds or minutes"] --> M3["Result updated each batch"]
    end
    subgraph ST["Event-at-a-time streaming"]
        S1["Event arrives"] --> S2["Processed immediately, per record"] --> S3["Result updated within milliseconds"]
    end
Model How it works Typical latency Examples
Batch Process a bounded dataset in one run, then stop Minutes to hours after the period closes Nightly finance loads, daily snapshots, model training
Micro-batch Treat a stream as a sequence of small batches, each covering new data since the last ~1 second to minutes Spark Structured Streaming (default mode), Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines streaming tables
Event-at-a-time (continuous) streaming Each record flows through the operators as it arrives Milliseconds Apache Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark's experimental continuous trigger

Real-time vs near-real-time

These words are abused. Use them precisely:

Term Honest meaning Typical tech
Hard real-time A missed deadline is a system failure (flight control, industrial control). Not a data-platform concern. Embedded systems
Real-time (in data) Sub-second end-to-end, per event Flink, Kafka Streams, in-memory stores
Near-real-time Seconds to a few minutes Spark micro-batch, streaming tables
Frequent batch Every 5–60 minutes Scheduled incremental jobs, availableNow triggers

Before building "real-time", ask what decision the consumer will make with the data and how fast they can act. A dashboard a human looks at twice a day does not need sub-second latency; a card-fraud check does.

3. OLTP vs OLAP processing

Covered in depth in chapter 01. As a processing type:

  • OLTP processing — short transactions touching few rows by key, high concurrency, strict consistency. You rarely build this as a data engineer; you read from it.
  • OLAP processing — long scans and aggregations over many rows and few columns. This is what Spark, Databricks SQL and warehouses are built for.
  • HTAP (hybrid) — some databases attempt both on one copy of data. Useful for operational analytics on fresh data, but they rarely replace a dedicated analytical platform for large history.

4. ETL vs ELT vs reverse ETL

---
title: ETL, ELT and reverse ETL — where the transform runs
---
flowchart LR
    subgraph ETL["ETL"]
        E1["Source"] --> E2["Transform engine<br/>(outside target)"] --> E3["Warehouse"]
    end
    subgraph ELT["ELT"]
        L1["Source"] --> L2["Lakehouse raw layer"] --> L3["Transform in place<br/>(SQL / Spark)"]
    end
    subgraph RETL["Reverse ETL"]
        R1["Gold tables"] --> R2["Sync tool"] --> R3["CRM, marketing,<br/>support tools"]
    end
ETL ELT Reverse ETL
Order Extract → transform → load Extract → load raw → transform inside platform Read modelled data → push to operational systems
Where compute runs A separate engine (SSIS, Informatica, custom code) The warehouse/lakehouse itself Sync tool or custom job
Raw data kept? Often not Yes (bronze) n/a
Strengths Sensitive data can be cleaned before landing; target stays small Reprocess any time from raw; one engine; SQL-friendly Puts analytics where business users work
Weaknesses Lost raw data; logic hidden in the tool Raw data (including PII) lands in the platform, so governance must be strong Another integration to monitor; must respect target API limits

Modern lakehouses are ELT by default. A nuance: pure ELT is rare. Even in a lakehouse you usually do light transformation at ingestion (add ingestion metadata, parse the envelope, mask a very sensitive field), so it is more precisely "EtLT".

5. Full load vs incremental load vs CDC

Strategy What each run reads Detects deletes? Cost as data grows When to use
Full load Entire source table Yes (anything missing was deleted) Grows linearly with table size Small tables (< a few million rows), reference data, sources with no reliable change column
Incremental (timestamp / high-watermark) Rows where modified_at > last_watermark No (deleted rows just disappear) Proportional to changes Sources with a trustworthy modified_at or increasing ID
CDC Change events (insert/update/delete) from the source Yes Proportional to changes Large, frequently updated tables; when deletes and every intermediate change matter

CDC flavours

Flavour Mechanism Pros Cons
Log-based Read the database's transaction log (SQL Server CDC, PostgreSQL logical replication, MySQL binlog) via tools like Debezium or managed connectors Captures every change including deletes; minimal load on source; ordered Needs DBA access and log retention; more moving parts
Trigger-based Database triggers write each change to a shadow/audit table Works on databases without log access Adds write overhead to every transaction; triggers are fragile
Timestamp / watermark-based ("query-based CDC") Poll with WHERE modified_at > :last Simple, no special permissions Misses deletes and intermediate updates between polls; relies on the application setting modified_at correctly

Timestamp-based polling has one classic trap: in-flight transactions. A row updated at 10:59:59 in a transaction that commits at 11:00:05 can be missed if your 11:00:00 run already moved the watermark to 10:59:59. Mitigate by reading with a small overlap (e.g. modified_at > last_watermark - 5 minutes) and deduplicating with a merge.

# Timestamp-based incremental extract with an overlap window
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

last_wm = spark.sql(
    "SELECT COALESCE(MAX(source_modified_at), TIMESTAMP'1900-01-01') AS wm FROM silver.customers"
).first()["wm"]

query = f"""
  (SELECT * FROM dbo.Customers
   WHERE ModifiedAt > DATEADD(minute, -5, '{last_wm:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S}')) AS src
"""

changes = (spark.read.format("jdbc")
           .option("url", jdbc_url)
           .option("dbtable", query)
           .load())
# ...then MERGE into silver keyed on CustomerId (see §6), so the overlap is harmless.

6. Append vs overwrite vs merge/upsert

Write mode Behaviour Idempotent on rerun? Typical layer
Append Add new rows only No — a rerun duplicates rows, unless you deduplicate or use transactional writes with an idempotency token Bronze, event logs
Overwrite (full) Replace the whole table Yes Small dimensions, full-load targets, gold rebuilds
Overwrite (partition / predicate) Replace only the slice being processed, e.g. one day Yes, per slice Daily facts, backfills
Merge / upsert Update matching keys, insert new ones, optionally delete Yes, if the source batch is deduplicated per key Silver entities, SCD, CDC targets 
-- Overwrite exactly one day, atomically (Delta Lake)
INSERT INTO gold.daily_sales
REPLACE WHERE sale_date = DATE'2026-09-24'
SELECT sale_date, store_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM silver.sales
WHERE sale_date = DATE'2026-09-24'
GROUP BY sale_date, store_id;

# The same thing in PySpark
(daily_df.write
    .format("delta")
    .mode("overwrite")
    .option("replaceWhere", "sale_date = '2026-09-24'")
    .saveAsTable("gold.daily_sales"))

-- Merge / upsert
MERGE INTO silver.customers AS t
USING staged_customer_changes AS s
  ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'DELETE' THEN INSERT *;

UPDATE SET * / INSERT * copy every column by name, so the staging table must have the same columns as the target. If s.op is not a column of the target, list the columns explicitly instead.

7. Lambda vs Kappa vs unified

---
title: Lambda vs Kappa architecture
---
flowchart LR
    subgraph LAMBDA["Lambda"]
        LS["Events"] --> LB["Batch layer<br/>recompute all history"]
        LS --> LSP["Speed layer<br/>stream, approximate"]
        LB --> LV["Serving layer<br/>merge both views"]
        LSP --> LV
    end
    subgraph KAPPA["Kappa"]
        KS["Durable log<br/>(Kafka)"] --> KP["One stream processor"] --> KV["Serving tables"]
        KS -.->|"replay to reprocess"| KP
    end
Lambda Kappa Unified lakehouse
Paths Batch + streaming Streaming only One engine, same code runs as batch or stream
Logic duplicated? Yes, two codebases that must agree No No
Reprocessing Rerun batch layer Replay the log (needs long retention) Rerun the same job over the Delta tables or a full refresh
Main pain Keeping two implementations consistent Replaying months of events is slow; log retention cost Needs a table format that supports both streaming reads and batch merges

Lambda was a workaround for streaming systems that could not be trusted for correctness. Kappa removed the duplication but made historical reprocessing depend on the log. The lakehouse approach (Structured Streaming over Delta tables, where the same DataFrame code runs as a stream or a batch) is effectively a pragmatic Kappa: the Delta table is the replayable log.

8. Scheduled vs event-triggered vs interactive

Invocation Description Example
Scheduled Runs on a clock (cron) Every day at 02:00 UTC
Event / file-arrival triggered Runs when data lands or an upstream finishes Databricks job with a file arrival trigger; ADF storage event trigger
Continuous Always running Streaming job with a processing-time trigger
Interactive / ad hoc A human runs a query or notebook to explore Analyst in a SQL editor; engineer debugging in a notebook

Interactive and scheduled workloads should run on different compute. Interactive clusters are sized for flexibility and stay up while people work; production jobs should use job compute or serverless that starts, runs and stops, which is both cheaper and isolates failures.

9. Stateless vs stateful stream processing

Stateless Stateful
Needs memory of earlier events? No Yes
Operations filter, select, withColumn, parse JSON, enrich with a static lookup Windowed aggregations, dropDuplicates over time, stream-stream joins, sessionisation
Checkpoint contents Offsets only Offsets plus state
Risk Low Unbounded state growth if there is no watermark

Rule: every stateful streaming operation needs a watermark (or a state TTL) so state can be dropped. Details in chapter 09.

10. Windowing

Window Shape Event belongs to Use case
Tumbling Fixed size, no overlap Exactly one window Orders per 5 minutes
Sliding (hopping) Fixed size, overlapping, advances by a slide interval Size ÷ slide windows "Last 10 minutes, updated every minute" moving metrics
Session Variable size per key, closes after a gap of inactivity One session per key User browsing sessions with a 30-minute timeout
Global Everything (no windowing) The single window Running totals (needs care with state) 
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

events = spark.readStream.table("bronze.clicks")

tumbling = (events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "5 minutes"), "page")
    .count())

sliding = (events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes", "1 minute"), "page")
    .count())

sessions = (events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "30 minutes")
    .groupBy(F.session_window("event_time", "30 minutes"), "user_id")
    .count())

11. Delivery guarantees

Guarantee Meaning How it happens Acceptable for
At-most-once Never duplicated, may be lost Commit progress before processing Metrics where loss is tolerable (sampling, debug logs)
At-least-once Never lost, may be duplicated Commit progress after processing; retry on failure Most pipelines, if the sink is idempotent
Exactly-once Each record's effect appears once Replayable source + checkpointed offsets + idempotent/transactional sink Financial and billing data, counts that must reconcile

"Exactly-once" is a property of the whole pipeline, not of one component. Kafka can offer exactly-once between Kafka topics; Spark offers exactly-once into Delta via checkpoints plus transactional commits. The moment you call an external API or write to a non-transactional sink inside the pipeline, you are back to at-least-once unless that sink deduplicates.

In practice most teams build at-least-once delivery + idempotent writes = effectively-once results.

12. Backfill and reprocessing

Backfill Reprocessing
Purpose Fill in periods never processed Recompute periods already processed
Trigger New table, new source, onboarding history Bug fix, logic change, upstream correction
Main risk Overloading sources, long runtimes Double counting, overwriting good data with bad
Safe technique Run the same idempotent job per partition/date range, in parallel batches Overwrite by partition (replaceWhere) or merge by key; never blind append

Design every job to accept a date range (or partition) parameter from day one. A job that can only process "yesterday" makes backfills painful. Patterns for doing this without double counting are in chapter 11.

13. Which processing type when

Requirement Recommended approach Latency Cost Complexity
Daily management reporting Scheduled batch, incremental, overwrite by date partition Hours Low Low
Finance close / regulatory reports Batch with full reconciliation, immutable snapshots Hours to days Low Medium (controls, audit)
Replicate an OLTP table to the lakehouse Log-based CDC → bronze append → silver merge Minutes Medium Medium
Small reference tables Full load, overwrite Hours Very low Very low
Operational dashboard (orders in the last hour) Micro-batch streaming or availableNow every few minutes Seconds to minutes Medium Medium
Fraud or anomaly alerting Low-latency streaming (Flink / Spark real-time options) Sub-second to seconds High High
Feature computation for ML training Batch, point-in-time correct joins Hours Low to medium Medium
Online feature serving Streaming updates into an online store Seconds High High
Pushing customer scores to a CRM Reverse ETL from gold, scheduled Hours Low Low to medium
Rebuilding history after a bug Reprocessing by partition, idempotent writes n/a One-off spike Medium

A good default for a new pipeline: incremental, idempotent, micro-batch capable, run on a schedule with availableNow. You get batch-like cost and operational simplicity, and you can shorten the schedule or switch to a continuous trigger later without rewriting logic.

Azure / .NET mapping

Processing type Azure option
Batch orchestration Azure Data Factory pipelines, Databricks Jobs
Micro-batch streaming Azure Databricks Structured Streaming, Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines
Low-latency stream processing Azure Stream Analytics, Flink on AKS/HDInsight, or Databricks
Streaming source Azure Event Hubs (Kafka endpoint)
Log-based CDC from SQL SQL Server / Azure SQL CDC feature, Debezium, ADF CDC resources
Cosmos DB changes Cosmos DB change feed
Reverse ETL target Dynamics 365, Azure SQL for app consumption

In .NET, the transactional outbox pattern produces clean domain events for downstream analytics: write the business row and an outbox row in one SQL transaction, then relay the outbox to Event Hubs. It is an application-level alternative to log-based CDC with explicit, contract-friendly event shapes.

Review checklist

  • I can place a pipeline on every axis in §1 and justify each choice.
  • I know the difference between micro-batch and event-at-a-time streaming and when each is justified.
  • I can explain why timestamp-based CDC misses deletes and how in-flight transactions can be missed.
  • I can say which write modes are idempotent and why append is not.
  • I can explain Lambda vs Kappa and why the lakehouse approach avoids duplicated logic.
  • I know that every stateful streaming operation needs a watermark.
  • I can explain why exactly-once is an end-to-end property.
  • Every job I design accepts a date range or partition parameter for backfills.
